source_title: Premium: The Hater's Guide To Megaspeed
other_side: Zitron, in a paid piece published the same day of which only the opening is free to read, does not see Washington seizing control of a private company. He sees overdue attention to conduct he says was reported for more than a year and ignored. He alleges Megaspeed is one part of a sprawling smuggling operation, and writes that Nvidia has "repeatedly and unashamedly profited from breaking the law". He repeats a short seller's claim that over a fifth of last fiscal year's revenue may have come from China-bound sales. These are his allegations; the free section does not discuss the chip-control bills.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether Nvidia knew its chips were reaching China. Both accept as fact that restricted chips got there in quantity, that Megaspeed was a large customer under investigation, and that Huang will be questioned under oath. The empirical question is what Nvidia's leadership knew and how much revenue was involved; the observable is the testimony, the documents Congress has asked to be preserved, and any Justice Department charges. The residue is worldview: whether this is the state asserting itself over a powerful company, or a company finally being held to existing law. For Whittemore to be vindicated, the lasting result must be political, with new chip laws and long hearings while markets move on. For Zitron, investigators must show knowing diversion on a scale that changes Nvidia's accounts. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both now say smuggling, not espionage, is the real issue. Watch Huang's testimony before Thanksgiving.
